title: Works and Days, Hesiod
subtitle: 8th century BC AD
subject: litterature
description: Hesiod speaks to his brother Perses: work, be fair, beware of excess. Between the myth of Pandora and the agricultural calendar, an ethic of work is born.

hero.hook: Before wisdom manuals, a farmer-poet lectures his brother.

blocks.text: Around the **8th century BC**, in , a region of central Greece north of Attica, the poet **Hesiod** wrote the **Works and the Days**. This is not an epic of warrior heroes. It is a poem addressed to his brother **Persès**, accused of having cheated on a family inheritance with the help of corrupt judges. [[Boeotia]]

Hesiod mixes myth, morality and agricultural advice. Working the land, respecting justice, avoiding pride: everyday life becomes poetic material. With Homer, his texts founded a large part of Greek mythology and reflection.

sections.title: A poet who speaks from his field

blocks.text: Unlike **Homer**, a semi-legendary figure of the epic poem, Hesiod puts himself on stage. He tells of his village, **Ashra**, a Boeotian locality, his father who came from Asia Minor, a region of present-day Türkiye, his trial against Perses. The **Muse**, inspiring goddess of the arts, chose him, he said. But the tone remains concrete: sow, reap, navigate at the right time.

blocks.caption: Hesiod: Greek poetry also descends into the fields.

blocks.text: This personal voice announces something modern: the author who gets involved, not just the anonymous bard. Hesiod speaks from the earth, not from the palace or the battlefield. He invents didactic poetry, poetry that teaches.

To explain the harshness of life, Hesiod tells **Prometheus**, titan who steals fire for men, and **Pandora**, first woman whose jar releases evils onto the world. He adds the [[five ages of humanity]]: gold, silver, bronze, hero, iron. We are living in the **Iron Age**, the worst, where justice falters and work is difficult.
, another great poem by the same author, tells of the birth of the gods from the **Chaos**, the original void. The Works come down from the sky towards the plow. [[Hesiod's Theogony]]

blocks.caption: Prometheus and fire: technical progress has a price, in Hesiod.

blocks.text: The moral heart of the poem opposes *Dikè*, justice, just order, to , the excess which pushes man to believe himself equal to the gods. Unjust kings are threatened by **Zeus**, king of the gods. The honest peasant has a chance. Hesiod does not promise paradise. He promises that effort is better than fraud. [[Hybris]]

The **work calendar** gives rhythm to the text: when to plow, when to harvest, when to be wary of the sea. Wisdom is seasonal. Knowing the rhythms of nature also means respecting an order larger than the appetite of the moment. Perses is lectured like a lazy brother, not like a king.

**Virgil**, Latin poet of the 1st century BC. BC, will be remembered in the [[Georgics]], an educational poem on agriculture. Moralists, from, a humanist of the Renaissance, to the moderns, read there an ethic of work. Hesiod is not gentle. It is clear: without work and justice, the community rots. [[Erasmus]]

Hesiod also speaks of the **good Eris**, goddess of useful rivalry who pushes the neighbor to work better, against the **bad Eris**, goddess of hatred and trial. In a harsh world, this distinction matters: emulation is not war. The poem thus becomes an art of living together, anchored in the seasons and measure.

The **Works and the Days** invent a poetry of everyday agricultural life. Hesiod said to his brother, and to us: cultivate your field, avoid excess, because the Iron Age does not forgive laziness or injustice.
